source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If the tangent drawn at $(\sqrt2,1)$ on the circle $x^2+y^2=3$ is also a tangent to the two circles of equal radius $2\sqrt3$ with centres at $(0,\beta_1)$ and $(0,\beta_2)$, then $|\beta_1-\beta_2|=$
explanation: Tangent: $\sqrt2x+y=3$. Distance from $(0,\beta)$: $\frac{|\beta-3|}{\sqrt3}=2\sqrt3\Rightarrow|\beta-3|=6$, so $\beta=9$ or $-3$ and $|\beta_1-\beta_2|=12$. Answer 6 is just $|\beta-3|$, not the difference of the two centres.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q49)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: The external centre of similitude of the two circles $x^2+y^2-4x+6y+4=0$ and $x^2+y^2-2x+2y-2=0$ is
explanation: $C_1=(2,-3),\ r_1=3$; $C_2=(1,-1),\ r_2=2$. External centre divides $C_1C_2$ externally in $3:2$: $\frac{3(1,-1)-2(2,-3)}{3-2}=(-1,3)$. Internal division gives $\left(\frac75,-\frac95\right)$; sign errors give the other options.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q50)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If $x^2+y^2-2x+2fy+c=0$ intersects the two circles $x^2+y^2+2x-4y+1=0$ and $x^2+y^2-4x-2y-11=0$ orthogonally, then $f+c=$
explanation: Orthogonality $2g_1g_2+2f_1f_2=c_1+c_2$ with $g=-1$: with the first circle $-2-4f=c+1$; with the second $4-2f=c-11$. Solving: $f=-9,\ c=33$, so $f+c=24$. Using $c_1-c_2$ on the right is the usual slip.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q51)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: PSQ is a focal chord of the parabola $y^2=12x$. A, B are respectively the feet of the perpendicular S drawn from P and Q on to the directrix of the parabola. If the length of AB is $7\sqrt3$ and $P=(3t^2,6t)\ (0<t<1)$, then $t=$
explanation: For a focal chord $Q=\left(\frac{3}{t^2},-\frac6t\right)$. $A,B$ on the directrix have the same $y$-coordinates as $P,Q$, so $AB=6\left(t+\frac1t\right)=7\sqrt3\Rightarrow t+\frac1t=\frac{7\sqrt3}{6}$, giving $t=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ or $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$. Since $0<t<1$, $t=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$; $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ is the rejected root.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q52)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: Let O, S be the vertex and focus of the parabola $y^2=4ax$ respectively and $x=k$ be its double ordinate of length $2\sqrt6a$. If the line $x=k$ cuts the X-axis at P, then length of the double ordinate drawn through O to the parabola having P and S as vertex and focus is
explanation: $4\sqrt{ak}=2\sqrt6a\Rightarrow k=\frac{3a}{2}$, so $P=\left(\frac{3a}{2},0\right)$, $S=(a,0)$. New parabola: vertex $P$, focal length $\frac a2$, opening left: $y^2=-2a\left(x-\frac{3a}{2}\right)$. At $x=0$: $y^2=3a^2$, so length $=2\sqrt3a$. $4\sqrt3a$ results from taking focal length $a$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q53)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If the distance between the foci of an ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is 6 and the distance between its directrices is 10, then the equation of one of the tangents of the ellipse drawn parallel to the line $y=\sqrt2x+5$ is
explanation: $ae=3$, $\frac ae=5\Rightarrow a^2=15$, $b^2=15-9=6$. Tangent $y=mx\pm\sqrt{a^2m^2+b^2}$ with $m=\sqrt2$: $\sqrt{30+6}=6$, so $y=\sqrt2x+6$. Using wrong $b^2$ (e.g. $a^2+(ae)^2$) produces the distractors.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q54)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: From a point $P(x_1,-1)\ (x_1<0)$, two tangents are drawn to the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{y^2}{3}=1$. If the sum of the slopes of the tangents is 2, then $x_1=$
explanation: Tangent $y=mx+c$ with $c^2=2m^2-3$; through $P$: $c=-1-mx_1$, so $(1+mx_1)^2=2m^2-3\Rightarrow(x_1^2-2)m^2+2x_1m+4=0$. Sum of slopes $\frac{-2x_1}{x_1^2-2}=2\Rightarrow x_1^2+x_1-2=0\Rightarrow x_1=1$ or $-2$. With $x_1<0$, $x_1=-2$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q55)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $A(1,2,1)$, $B\left(\frac95,\frac85,\frac95\right)$, $C(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and $D(-3,4,-3)$ be four collinear points. If $B$ divides $AC$ in the ratio of $m:n$, $D$ divides $AC$ in the ratio $m:-n$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=$
explanation: Write points as $A+t(-4,2,-4)$: $A\to0$, $D\to1$, $B\to-\frac15$, $C\to c$. $B,D$ divide $AC$ internally and externally in the same ratio (harmonic conjugates): $\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{AD}{DC}\Rightarrow\frac{1/5}{-1/5-c}=\frac{1}{1-c}\Rightarrow c=-\frac12$. So $C=(3,1,3)$ and $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=7$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q56)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: The acute angle between the lines whose direction cosines satisfy the relations $l^2-5m^2+n^2=0$ and $l+m-n=0$ is
explanation: $n=l+m\Rightarrow l^2-5m^2+(l+m)^2=0\Rightarrow l^2+lm-2m^2=0\Rightarrow(l-m)(l+2m)=0$. Direction ratios $(1,1,2)$ and $(-2,1,-1)$: $\cos\theta=\frac{|-2+1-2|}{\sqrt6\sqrt6}=\frac12$, so $\theta=\frac\pi3$. $\frac\pi6$ confuses $\cos$ with $\sin$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q57)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: $A(3,1,2)$, $B(-1,6,2)$ and $C(1,1,-2)$ are three points. A plane is passing through $A$ and is perpendicular to the line joining $B$ and $C$. If $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is the image of $C$ with respect to the plane, then $3\alpha-\gamma+2\beta=$
explanation: Normal $\vec{BC}=(2,-5,-4)$; plane $2x-5y-4z+7=0$. For $C$: value $2-5+8+7=12$. Image $=C-\frac{2\cdot12}{45}(2,-5,-4)=\left(-\frac1{15},\frac{11}{3},\frac2{15}\right)$. Then $3\alpha-\gamma+2\beta=-\frac15-\frac2{15}+\frac{22}{3}=7$. Using the foot of the perpendicular (factor 1 instead of 2) gives a wrong value.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q58)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix}2+\frac{\sin x}{x}&1&3\\2&1+\frac{\sin x}{x}&3\\2&1&3+\frac{\sin x}{x}\end{vmatrix}$, then $\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=$
explanation: As $x\to0$, $\frac{\sin x}{x}\to1$, so the limit is $\begin{vmatrix}3&1&3\\2&2&3\\2&1&4\end{vmatrix}=3(5)-1(2)+3(-2)=7$. Treating $\frac{\sin x}{x}\to0$ gives the determinant of the constant matrix, $0$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q59)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: The number of points of discontinuity of the function $f(x)=[x]+|x-2|$, $-3<x<3$ is
explanation: $|x-2|$ is continuous everywhere; $[x]$ jumps at every integer in $(-3,3)$: $-2,-1,0,1,2$. So 5 points. The endpoints $\pm3$ are excluded, and $|x-2|$ only affects differentiability at $x=2$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q60)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If $f$ is a derivable function and $2f(\sin x)+f(\cos x)=x$ for all $x\in R$, then $f'(x)=$
explanation: Replace $x$ by $\frac\pi2-x$: $2f(\cos x)+f(\sin x)=\frac\pi2-x$. Eliminating $f(\cos x)$: $3f(\sin x)=3x-\frac\pi2\Rightarrow f(t)=\sin^{-1}t-\frac\pi6$. Hence $f'(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$. $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ is the reciprocal trap.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q62)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If $y=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+x+x^2}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{x^2+3x+3}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{x^2+5x+7}\right)$, then $y'(0)=$
explanation: Denominators are $1+x(x+1)$, $1+(x+1)(x+2)$, $1+(x+2)(x+3)$, so the sum telescopes: $y=\tan^{-1}(x+3)-\tan^{-1}x$. Then $y'=\frac{1}{1+(x+3)^2}-\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ and $y'(0)=\frac1{10}-1=-\frac9{10}$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q63)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}\int_3^x\left(2t-3f'(t)\right)dt$, then $f'(3)=$
explanation: $x^2f(x)=\int_3^x(2t-3f'(t))dt$, so $f(3)=0$. Differentiating: $2xf(x)+x^2f'(x)=2x-3f'(x)$. At $x=3$: $9f'(3)=6-3f'(3)\Rightarrow f'(3)=\frac12$. Forgetting the $-3f'$ term gives $\frac23$; sign slips give $-\frac12$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q64)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: A particle is moving on a straight line so that its distance $s$ from a fixed point at any time $t$ is proportional to $t^n$. If $v$ is the velocity and '$a$' is the accelation of the particle at any time $t$, then $\frac{nas}{n-1}=$
explanation: $s=kt^n$, $v=nkt^{n-1}$, $a=n(n-1)kt^{n-2}$. Then $\frac{nas}{n-1}=n\cdot nkt^{n-2}\cdot kt^n=n^2k^2t^{2n-2}=v^2$. The expression is quadratic in $k$, so linear options like $3v$ or $4v$ cannot match dimensionally.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q65)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: The closest point on the parabola $y=x^2+7x+2$ to the straight line $y=3x-2$ is
explanation: The closest point has tangent parallel to the line: $2x+7=3\Rightarrow x=-2$, $y=4-14+2=-8$. (In fact $x^2+7x+2-(3x-2)=(x+2)^2$, so the line touches the parabola at $(-2,-8)$, distance 0.) Other options lie on the parabola but at positive distance from the line.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q66)

subject: mathematics
stem: If $y=a\log|x|+bx^2+x$ has its extremum values at $x=-1$ and $x=2$, then $(a,b)=$
explanation: $y'=\frac ax+2bx+1$. $y'(-1)=0\Rightarrow -a-2b+1=0$; $y'(2)=0\Rightarrow\frac a2+4b+1=0$. Solving: $b=-\frac12$, $a=2$. Sign slips when differentiating $\log|x|$ for negative $x$ lead to the other pairs.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q67)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: The function $f(x)=2x+\cot^{-1}x+\log\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}-x\right)$
explanation: $f'(x)=2-\frac1{1+x^2}-\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$ (since $\frac{d}{dx}\log(\sqrt{1+x^2}-x)=-\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$). With $u=\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\in(0,1]$, $f'=2-u^2-u\ge0$, equality only at $x=0$. So $f$ increases on $\mathbb R$. Forgetting the minus sign in $\frac{d}{dx}\cot^{-1}x$ would mislead.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q68)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If $\int\frac{2\cos x+3\sin x}{3\cos x+4\sin x}dx=Ax+B\log|3\cos x+4\sin x|+c$, then $A\cdot B=$
explanation: Write $2\cos x+3\sin x=A(3\cos x+4\sin x)+B(4\cos x-3\sin x)$: $3A+4B=2$, $4A-3B=3\Rightarrow A=\frac{18}{25}$, $B=-\frac1{25}$. So $AB=-\frac{18}{625}$. Getting $B$ positive (sign of derivative) gives $\frac{18}{625}$; $\pm\frac{18}{25}$ forgets one denominator.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q69)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: If $\int\frac{1}{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}dx=A\log\left|\frac{\sqrt2+t}{\sqrt2-t}\right|+B\tan^{-1}(t)+c$, then $\left(\frac BA,t\right)=$
explanation: $\sin^3x+\cos^3x=(s+c)(1-sc)$. Multiply by $(s+c)$ and put $t=\sin x-\cos x$: $dt=(s+c)dx$, $(s+c)^2=2-t^2$, $1-sc=\frac{1+t^2}{2}$. Integral $=\int\frac{2\,dt}{(2-t^2)(1+t^2)}=\frac23\int\left(\frac1{2-t^2}+\frac1{1+t^2}\right)dt$, so $A=\frac1{3\sqrt2}$, $B=\frac23$, $\frac BA=2\sqrt2$. $t=\sin x+\cos x$ would not give $\tan^{-1}$ form.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q70)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
explanation: $\frac{d}{dx}4^{4^{4^x}}=4^{4^{4^x}}\ln4\cdot4^{4^x}\ln4\cdot4^x\ln4$ (chain rule thrice), so the integrand is $\frac{1}{(\ln4)^3}\frac{d}{dx}4^{4^{4^x}}$ and $A=\frac1{(\ln4)^3}$. Counting only one or two $\ln4$ factors gives the other options.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q71)

subject: mathematics
stem: If $\int\frac{dx}{2\sin^2x+\sin2x}=\frac12\log|f(x)|+c$ and $f\left(\frac\pi4\right)=\frac12$, then $f(x)=$
explanation: Divide by $\cos^2x$: $\int\frac{\sec^2x\,dx}{2\tan^2x+2\tan x}$; with $t=\tan x$: $\frac12\int\left(\frac1t-\frac1{t+1}\right)dt=\frac12\log\left|\frac{\tan x}{1+\tan x}\right|+c$. Check $f\left(\frac\pi4\right)=\frac12$ fixes the constant multiple as 1. The $\cot$ form gives $\frac12$ at $\frac\pi4$ too but its derivative has the wrong sign.

stem: If $\int e^x\frac{x^3+3x^2+4}{(x+1)^3}dx=e^xf(x)+c$, then $f(x)=$

subject: mathematics
stem: The area of the region enclosed between the curve $y=\log_e(x+e)$ and the coordinate axes is
explanation: The curve meets the $x$-axis at $x=1-e$ and the $y$-axis at $y=1$. Area $=\int_{1-e}^0\ln(x+e)dx=\int_1^e\ln u\,du=[u\ln u-u]_1^e=1$. Integrating up to $x=e$ or forgetting the lower limit gives larger values.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q74)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1+2^4+3^4+\cdots+n^4}{n^5}-\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1+2^3+3^3+\cdots+n^3}{n^5}=$
explanation: $\sum k^4\sim\frac{n^5}{5}$, so the first limit is $\int_0^1x^4dx=\frac15$. $\sum k^3=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}\sim\frac{n^4}{4}$, so divided by $n^5$ it tends to 0. Answer $\frac15$. $\frac1{20}=\frac14-\frac15$ is the trap of treating the second limit as $\frac14$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q75)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: $\int_{1/e}^{e^2}\left|\frac{\log_ex}{x}\right|dx=$
explanation: $\log x<0$ on $(1/e,1)$. $\int_{1/e}^1-\frac{\ln x}{x}dx=\left[-\frac{(\ln x)^2}{2}\right]_{1/e}^1=\frac12$; $\int_1^{e^2}\frac{\ln x}{x}dx=\frac{4}{2}=2$. Total $\frac52$. Ignoring the modulus gives $2-\frac12=\frac32$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q76)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
explanation: $x^3+3x^2+3x+3=(x+1)^3+2$. Put $u=x+1\in[-1,1]$: $\int_{-1}^1\left(u^3+2+u\cos u\right)du$. $u^3$ and $u\cos u$ are odd, so the integral is $\int_{-1}^12\,du=4$. Using $+3$ instead of $+2$ (not completing the cube) gives 6.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q77)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: The order and degree of the differential equation $\left\{1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right\}^{3/2}=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ are respectively
explanation: Highest derivative is $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$: order 2. Squaring to remove the fractional power: $\left(1+y'^2\right)^3=(y'')^2$, so degree 2. Reading the degree as $3$ (from the cube) or $\frac32$ ignores that degree is the power of the highest-order derivative after rationalising.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q78)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=ye^x$ is such that when $x=0,y=e$. The value of $y\ (y>0)$ when $x=1$ will be
explanation: Separate: $\ln y=e^x+C$. At $x=0$: $1=1+C\Rightarrow C=0$, so $y=e^{e^x}$ and $y(1)=e^e$. Answer $e$ is the initial value; forgetting that $e^0=1$ gives wrong constants.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q79)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: mathematics
stem: The general solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac yx=x^2$ is
explanation: Linear DE with integrating factor $x$: $\frac{d}{dx}(xy)=x^3\Rightarrow xy=\frac{x^4}{4}+c\Rightarrow y=\frac{x^3}{4}+\frac cx$. Option A forgets to divide $\frac{x^4}{4}$ by $x$ correctly; option C drops the $\frac1x$ on the constant.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q80)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: If A, B and C represent the work done, distance and electric charge respectively, then the physical quantity having the dimensions of $\dfrac{C^2}{AB}$ is
explanation: $\dfrac{C^2}{AB}$ has units $\dfrac{\mathrm{C^2}}{\mathrm{N\,m}\cdot\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}m^{-2}}$, the unit of permittivity (from $F=\dfrac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$). Electric potential is $A/C$ and electric energy is $A$ itself; permeability has units $\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q81)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A balloon is rising vertically upwards with a velocity of $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. When the balloon is at a height of 40 m from the ground, a stone is dropped from it. The time taken by the stone to reach the ground is (Acceleration due to gravity $=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$)
explanation: The stone starts with the balloon's velocity $+10\ \mathrm{m/s}$ upward. Taking up as positive: $-40=10t-5t^2\Rightarrow t^2-2t-8=0\Rightarrow t=4$ s. Ignoring the initial upward velocity gives $t=2\sqrt2$ s (not an option); other options come from arithmetic slips.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q82)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A swimmer can swim at $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in still water. River flows at $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. To cross the river in shortest time, the angle with respect to perpendicular to the flow is
explanation: Crossing time $t=\dfrac{d}{v\cos\theta}$ is minimum when $\theta=0^\circ$, i.e., swimming perpendicular to the flow. $\sin^{-1}(3/5)$ (upstream) is the trap: that is the heading for the shortest path (no drift), not shortest time.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q83)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: If $a=-kv$ represents the variation of acceleration of a particle with velocity, time taken to reduce the velocity from $v$ to $v/2$ is
explanation: $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-kv\Rightarrow \int_v^{v/2}\dfrac{dv}{v}=-k t\Rightarrow \ln\dfrac12=-kt\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{\ln2}{k}$. Treating the deceleration as constant gives $\dfrac{1}{2k}$, which is wrong since $a$ changes with $v$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q84)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A stream of water flowing horizontally with a speed of $15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gushes out of a tube of cross-sectional area $10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and hits a vertical wall nearby. Assuming water does not rebound, the force exerted on the wall by the impact of water is
explanation: Mass per second $=\rho A v=1000\times10^{-2}\times15=150\ \mathrm{kg/s}$. Force $=\rho Av^2=150\times15=2250\ \mathrm{N}=2.25\times10^3$ N. Using $\rho Av$ alone gives 150 (momentum rate omitted); forgetting $\rho=1000$ gives 2.25 N.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q85)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ block on a rough incline of $37^\circ$ is connected (by a string over a pulley at the top of the incline) to a hanging mass of $4\ \mathrm{kg}$. If the coefficient of friction between the 3 kg block and the rough incline is $\mu=0.25$, then the acceleration of the system is $[g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\ \sin37^\circ=0.6,\ \cos37^\circ=0.8]$
explanation: Hanging mass pulls with 40 N; the 3 kg block (moving up the incline) resists with $mg\sin37^\circ=18$ N and friction $\mu mg\cos37^\circ=6$ N. $a=\dfrac{40-18-6}{3+4}=\dfrac{16}{7}\approx2.28\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Ignoring friction gives $22/7\approx3.1$; dividing by 4 kg only or adding friction wrongly gives other values.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q86)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ car moves at $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Power required to maintain speed against $500\ \mathrm{N}$ resistive force is
explanation: At constant speed the engine force equals the resistance: $P=Fv=500\times20=10^4\ \mathrm{W}=10$ kW. The mass is irrelevant (no acceleration); using $mg$ or kinetic energy gives the wrong options.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q87)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A massless spring with a spring constant $k$ is fixed at its upper end. A block of mass $M$ is attached to the lower end of the spring and released from rest in its unstretched position. The maximum elongation of the spring is
explanation: At maximum elongation the block is momentarily at rest: $Mgx=\tfrac12kx^2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{2Mg}{k}$. $\dfrac{Mg}{k}$ is the equilibrium extension (reached only if lowered slowly), the common trap.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q88)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The rotational kinetic energy of a solid sphere of mass 3 kg and radius 0.2 m rolling down an inclined plane of height 7 m is (nearer to)
explanation: Total KE at bottom $=mgh=3\times10\times7=210$ J. For a rolling solid sphere $K_{rot}:K_{total}=\tfrac25:\tfrac75=2:7$, so $K_{rot}=210\times\tfrac27=60$ J. Using the ring/disc ratio or taking the translational share (150 J) gives wrong answers.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q89)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two particles of masses 4 g and 2 g are separated by a distance of 60 cm. The center of mass of the system of these two particles

options.text: Lies at a distance of 30 cm from 4 g particle
Lies at a distance of 40 cm from 4 g particle
Lies at a distance of 40 cm from 2 g particle
Lies at a distance of 20 cm from 2 g particle

explanation: From the 4 g particle: $x=\dfrac{2\times60}{4+2}=20$ cm, hence $60-20=40$ cm from the 2 g particle. The COM lies closer to the heavier mass; option (2) swaps the distances.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q90)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A particle is executing simple harmonic motion with amplitude $A$. The position at which kinetic energy and potential energy are equal is given by
explanation: $U=\tfrac12kx^2$ and $K=\tfrac12k(A^2-x^2)$. Setting $K=U$: $x^2=A^2/2\Rightarrow x=A/\sqrt2$. At $x=A/2$, $U$ is only one-quarter of total energy.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q91)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The displacement of a particle executing simple harmonic motion is given by $x=6\sin\left(2\pi t+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ m. The amplitude and maximum speed are given by
explanation: Amplitude $A=6$ m, $\omega=2\pi\ \mathrm{rad/s}$, so $v_{max}=A\omega=12\pi\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Option (2) mistakes $v_{max}$ as $2\omega$ or similar; the phase $\pi/4$ does not affect either value.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q92)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: When $g$ is acceleration due to gravity on earth, the gain in potential energy of an object of mass $m$ raised from the surface of earth to a height equal to the radius of earth $R$ is given by
explanation: $\Delta U=-\dfrac{GMm}{2R}+\dfrac{GMm}{R}=\dfrac{GMm}{2R}=\dfrac{mgR}{2}$ (using $GM=gR^2$). Using $mgh$ with $h=R$ gives $mgR$, which is wrong because $g$ decreases with height.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q93)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The pressure applied on a cube from all sides is $P$. In order to keep its volume constant, the temperature of cube is to be raised by (The Bulk modulus and the coefficient of volume expansion of the material of the cube are $\beta$ and $\alpha$ respectively)
explanation: Compression: $\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}=\dfrac{P}{\beta}$. Thermal expansion must cancel it: $\alpha\Delta T=\dfrac{P}{\beta}\Rightarrow\Delta T=\dfrac{P}{\alpha\beta}$. The other options misplace $\alpha$ or $\beta$; a quick dimension check ($\Delta T$ in K) eliminates them.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q94)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A small sphere of radius $r$ is dropped in a viscous liquid. When it is moving with terminal velocity in the liquid, the relation between the rate of heat produced $\left(\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\right)$ and $r$ is
explanation: Heat rate = power against viscous drag: $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=Fv_t=6\pi\eta r v_t^2$. Since $v_t\propto r^2$, $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\propto r\cdot r^4=r^5$. Option (1) uses $v_t\propto r^2$ alone, forgetting the drag force factor.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q95)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two rods made of metals A and B, each of length 20 cm, expand by 0.075 cm and 0.045 cm respectively, when heated from $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$. A composite rod of same length is made with a portion of metal A and remaining with B expands by 0.060 cm for same rise of temperature. Then the portion of composite rod made of A has initial length
explanation: Expansion per cm: A $=0.075/20$, B $=0.045/20$. With length $x$ of A: $\dfrac{0.075x+0.045(20-x)}{20}=0.060\Rightarrow0.03x=0.3\Rightarrow x=10$ cm. Since 0.060 is exactly midway between 0.075 and 0.045, the rod is half A, half B.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q96)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: An ideal gas is expanding such that $P^2T=$ constant. The coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is ($P$ - Pressure, $T$ - temperature of the gas)
explanation: $P\propto T/V$, so $P^2T\propto T^3/V^2=$ const $\Rightarrow V\propto T^{3/2}$. Then $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{V}\dfrac{dV}{dT}=\dfrac{3}{2T}$. $\dfrac1T$ holds only for an isobaric process.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q97)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The efficiency of Carnot engine is 50% and temperature of sink is 500 K. Keeping the source temperature constant, the required sink temperature to raise the efficiency of the engine to 60% is
explanation: $0.5=1-\dfrac{500}{T_1}\Rightarrow T_1=1000$ K. For 60%: $T_2=(1-0.6)\times1000=400$ K. Efficiency rises only if the sink is cooled, so 500 K and 600 K are impossible.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q99)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two moles of Helium are mixed with $n$ moles of Hydrogen. The rms speed of the gas molecules in the mixture is $\sqrt2$ times the speed of sound in the mixture. The value of $n$ is
explanation: $\dfrac{v_{rms}}{v_s}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{\gamma}}=\sqrt2\Rightarrow\gamma=\dfrac32$, so $C_V=\dfrac{R}{\gamma-1}=2R$. Mixture: $C_V=\dfrac{2\cdot\frac32R+n\cdot\frac52R}{2+n}=2R\Rightarrow3+2.5n=4+2n\Rightarrow n=2$. Averaging $\gamma$ directly instead of $C_V$ leads to wrong values.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q100)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two vibrating tuning forks produce progressive waves given by $y_1=2\sin(500\pi t-ax)$ and $y_2=2\sin(506\pi t-bx)$. Number of beats produced per minute is
explanation: $f_1=\dfrac{500\pi}{2\pi}=250$ Hz, $f_2=253$ Hz. Beat frequency $=3$ per second $=180$ per minute. Using $\omega$ difference directly ($6\pi$) or forgetting to convert to per minute gives 360 or 3.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q101)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A convex lens forms a real image 4 cm long on a screen. When the lens is shifted to a new position without disturbing the object, again a real image is formed on the screen which is 16 cm tall. The length of the object must be
explanation: In the displacement method the two positions interchange $u$ and $v$, so $m_1m_2=1$ and $h_o=\sqrt{h_1h_2}=\sqrt{4\times16}=8$ cm. The arithmetic mean (10 cm) or sum (20 cm) are traps.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q102)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A vessel of depth $x$ is half filled with oil of refractive index $\mu_1$ and the other half is filled with water of refractive index $\mu_2$. The apparent depth of the vessel when viewed from above is
explanation: Apparent depths add: $\dfrac{x/2}{\mu_1}+\dfrac{x/2}{\mu_2}=\dfrac{x(\mu_1+\mu_2)}{2\mu_1\mu_2}$. Options (2) and (3) invert the combination of $\mu$'s; (3) would even exceed the real depth $x$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q103)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The direction of the second order diffraction minima in Fraunhofer diffraction at a single slit is ($a$ = slit width) given by
explanation: Single-slit minima: $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$; for $n=2$, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2\lambda}{a}$. Option (1) confuses with half-wavelength conditions; (3) and (4) are dimensionally wrong.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q104)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Charges $q$, $2q$, $3q$ and $4q$ are placed at the corners A, B, C and D of a square respectively (A bottom-left, B bottom-right, C top-right, D top-left). The direction of electric field at the centre O of the square is along
explanation: Opposite charges on each diagonal partly cancel. Along AC: net field $\propto 3q-q=2q$ pointing from C towards A. Along BD: net $\propto 4q-2q=2q$ pointing from D towards B. These equal fields at $90^\circ$ add to a resultant pointing straight down, i.e., parallel to CB. AC or BD alone gives only one diagonal's contribution.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q105)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The electrical potential at a point A in an electric field $300\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ is 900 V. Now find the work done in moving $1\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ charge from point A to 10 m (from the source charge) is
explanation: For a point source, $V/E=r\Rightarrow r_A=900/300=3$ m, so $kQ=2700$ V m. At 10 m, $V=270$ V. Work done by the field $=q(V_A-V)=10^{-6}\times(900-270)=630\times10^{-6}$ J. Using $W=qEd$ with a uniform field ignores that the field falls as $1/r^2$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q106)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Two point charges, $+2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and $-2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$, are fixed respectively at points A and B, separated by 4 m in air. A point P is located such that it is 3 m from $+2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and 5 m from $-2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$. What is the electric potential at point P? Take $k=9\times10^9\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}$
explanation: Potential is a scalar sum: $V=9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-6}\left(\dfrac13-\dfrac15\right)=18000\times\dfrac{2}{15}=2400$ V. Taking only the negative charge ($-3600$ V) or mishandling signs gives the other options.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q107)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A resistor has three colour bands, Orange, Red and Black from left to right respectively, the value of resistance is
explanation: Orange = 3, Red = 2, Black multiplier $=10^0$: $R=32\times1=32\ \Omega$. Treating black as a zero digit gives $320\ \Omega$, the common trap; the third band is the multiplier.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q109)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: The radius of a coil of wire with $N$ turns is 0.1 m and 2 A current flows in the coil. A long straight wire carrying a current of $20\pi$ A is located at 0.5 m from the centre of the coil, with the current directions such that their fields at the centre are opposite. The number of turns in the coil if the resultant magnetic field at the centre of the coil is zero
explanation: Wire: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}=\dfrac{\mu_0\cdot20\pi}{2\pi\cdot0.5}=20\mu_0$. Coil: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2r}=\dfrac{\mu_0N\cdot2}{0.2}=10N\mu_0$. Equating, $N=2$. Using $\mu_0NI/r$ (dropping the 2) or other formula slips gives the other options.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q110)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A charged particle moves in a region where there is a uniform electric field $\vec E=2\times10^3\,\hat i\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ and a uniform magnetic field $\vec B=5\times10^{-2}\,\hat j$ T. The velocity of the particle (in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$), if the particle moves without any acceleration, is
explanation: No acceleration: $\vec E+\vec v\times\vec B=0\Rightarrow\vec v=\dfrac{\vec E\times\vec B}{B^2}$. $|v|=\dfrac{2\times10^3}{5\times10^{-2}}=4\times10^4$ m/s, direction $\hat i\times\hat j=\hat k$ (independent of the sign of charge). $-\hat k$ would make the forces add instead of cancel.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q111)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: At a given place the ratio of total magnetic field of earth to the horizontal component of earth's field is 2. Angle of dip at that place is
explanation: $B_H=B\cos\delta\Rightarrow\cos\delta=\dfrac{1}{2}\Rightarrow\delta=60^\circ$. Using $\sin\delta=1/2$ (confusing with the vertical component) gives $30^\circ$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q112)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: A loop moves towards a stationary magnet at constant speed $V$ resulting in an induced emf $E$ within the loop. If the magnet also moves away from the loop at the same speed $V$, the new induced emf in the loop is
explanation: Induced emf depends on relative motion. Both move in the same direction at speed $V$, so their separation stays constant, flux does not change and emf $=0$. $2E$ would apply if the magnet moved towards the loop.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q113)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: An alternating supply of $225$ V is applied across a circuit with resistance $20\ \Omega$ and impedance of $45\ \Omega$. The power dissipated in the circuit is
explanation: $I_{rms}=\dfrac{225}{45}=5$ A; power is dissipated only in the resistance: $P=I^2R=25\times20=500$ W. Using $V^2/R$ or $VI$ (1125 W) ignores the power factor $R/Z$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q114)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: Electromagnetic radiations are emitted from a 15 W point source. The peak value of the magnetic field at a distance of 5 m from the source is
explanation: $I=\dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}=\dfrac{15}{100\pi}$ W/m$^2$. $I=\dfrac{cB_0^2}{2\mu_0}\Rightarrow B_0=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\mu_0I}{c}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times4\pi\times10^{-7}\times15}{100\pi\times3\times10^8}}=\sqrt{4\times10^{-16}}=2\times10^{-8}$ T. Forgetting the factor 2 (rms vs peak) changes the value by $\sqrt2$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q115)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: When photons of energy 4.2 eV are incident on a photosensitive material of work function 2.2 eV, photoelectrons are emitted with a maximum linear momentum of $P$. If photons of energy 6.2 eV are incident on the same photosensitive material, the maximum linear momentum of the emitted photoelectrons is
explanation: $K_{max}$ goes from $4.2-2.2=2$ eV to $6.2-2.2=4$ eV. Since $p=\sqrt{2mK}$, momentum scales as $\sqrt2$: $P\sqrt2$. Taking $p\propto K$ gives $2P$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q116)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: If the ratio of the time periods of the electrons revolving in the first and $n^{th}$ orbits of Hydrogen atom is $1:64$, then the angular momentum of the electron in the $n^{th}$ excited state of Hydrogen atom is ($h$ - Planck's constant)
explanation: $T\propto n^3\Rightarrow n^3=64\Rightarrow n=4$. The 4th excited state is the 5th orbit, so $L=\dfrac{5h}{2\pi}=\dfrac{2.5h}{\pi}$. Using the 4th orbit itself ($\dfrac{4h}{2\pi}=\dfrac{2h}{\pi}$) is the trap: excited states are counted above the ground state $n=1$.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q117)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: If the radius of a nucleus having 13 protons and 14 neutrons is 3.6 fm, then the ratio of the volume to surface area of nucleus having 53 protons and 72 neutrons is
explanation: $R\propto A^{1/3}$: $R=3.6\left(\dfrac{125}{27}\right)^{1/3}=3.6\times\dfrac53=6$ fm. For a sphere $\dfrac{V}{S}=\dfrac{R}{3}=2$ fm. 6 fm is the radius itself, the common trap.

source.name: AP EAPCET 2026 (official master paper with preliminary key, 14 May Shift 2, Q118)
source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice

subject: physics
stem: In amplitude modulation, if the modulation index is 0.8 and the peak voltage of the message signal is 10 V, then the amplitudes of the upper and lower side bands of the modulated wave are respectively
explanation: $A_c=\dfrac{A_m}{\mu}=\dfrac{10}{0.8}=12.5$ V. Each side band has amplitude $\dfrac{\mu A_c}{2}=\dfrac{A_m}{2}=5$ V, and both side bands are equal. Unequal pairs are wrong; 22.5 V and 2.5 V are $A_c\pm A_m$ (max/min envelope).

source.licence: Official exam-authority release; for personal practice
